https://www.dw.com/en/the-slovak-village.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Hs7W Some residents of Vlkolinec would like their picturesque village's designation as a UNESCO World Heritage site to be revoked Image: Rob Cameron/DW Advertisement From the headlines in the world's media, the story seemed simple: A tiny Slovak village wanted UNESCO to remove it from the World Heritage List because of the pressures of overtourism . But that's not quite what is happening in Vlkolinec, central Slovakia . Interviews with residents, local officials and visitors suggest that the debate was less about UNESCO itself than about how to protect a living community from the pressures of tourism . Accelerated transformation "Those who come with humility, to admire the village and understand how people lived here, are always welcome," said 68-year-old Anton Sabucha. "They don't bother me. It's the rude ones." Sitting beneath an awning outside his wooden house, Sabucha leafed through a history of the village, pointing to photographs of neighbors and relatives. His wife brought out a tray of fried dough pastries. Vlkolinec in bygone days: Anton Sabucha says that the village's inscription on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1993 accelerated its transformation Image: Haris Jeelani Toogo/DW He remembered when around 200 people lived in Vlkolinec. Today, only 17 remain year-round. UNESCO did not create Vlkolinec's tourism problem. The village was designated a Folk Architecture Heritage Reserve in 1977, during the Communist era . But Sabucha argued that its inscription on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1993 accelerated the transformation, bringing visitors who too often forget that people still live in the centuries-old wooden houses. Diminishing privacy "You come out into your yard, wanting to sit quietly and have a coffee with your friends. Then the first tourist comes and asks, 'How are you? What's it like living here?' Then another. Then another," he told DW. Sabucha has erected a barrier at the entrance to his property bearing the notices "No Trespassing" and "No Photos." He said that despite this, some visitors still wander into private gardens, trampling flowers and treating the village as an attraction rather than a community. Vlkolinec resident Anton Sabucha says that some tourists often forget that people still live in the centuries-old wooden houses they come to admire Image: Haris Jeelani Toogo/DW "Someone sees the 'No Photos' sign and still has to take a picture. They simply don't respect people's privacy." Disappearance of traditional village life But the biggest loss, he said, has been the gradual disappearance of traditional village life. The surrounding meadows are no longer cut, the old agricultural terraces have become overgrown and many of the people whose lives have shaped the landscape are gone. Tourism income, he argued, has done little to reverse that decline. Residents receive around €400 ($455) a year from ticket revenues — "barely enough to buy a pallet of briquettes for the winter" — while many of those who now earn a living from tourism no longer live in the village, he said. "For an ordinary tourist, these are just wooden houses. For us, they're people. We know exactly who lived in each house." A living village Justine, a tourist visiting from France , said the village's appeal lay precisely in the fact that people still lived there. "Usually places like this are museums. Here, people still live here. That's unique," she told DW. When told that some residents wanted Vlkolinec removed from the UNESCO list because of tourism, she said she understood their frustration. Slovak village debates UNESCO status over tourism To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video "Having people walking around your village every day could become unpleasant," she said. "But at the same time, tourism also supports the region. It's difficult to know what's best." UNESCO status helps preservation Not everyone agrees that UNESCO is the problem. Miro Parobek, who oversees tourism for the town of Ruzomberok, which administers Vlkolinec as a municipal district, acknowledged that tourism had brought challenges. But he argued that the answer was better management, not removing the village from the World Heritage List. "Our first priority is to preserve the traditional architecture," Parobek told DW. "But our goal is also for this to remain a living village. We want to support the people who live here." He said the town had already responded to residents' concerns by replacing large festivals with smaller cultural events, while residents now met regularly with local officials through a dedicated working group. Miro Pirobek, head of Culture and Tourism in the nearby town of Ruzomberok, says that the priority is to preserve the traditional architecture of the village and support the people who live there Image: Haris Jeelani Toogo/DW The municipality also helped homeowners apply for grants to restore historical buildings and even provided twice-weekly transport into nearby Ruzomberok for older residents. Parobek said every entrance ticket carried the same message: "Vlkolinec is not an open-air museum. Please respect the privacy of the people who live here." Balancing tourism, heritage and residents' wishes He acknowledged that the balance between protecting residents and welcoming visitors was not always easy. Much of Parobek's optimism rested on plans that had yet to materialize. Ruzomberok was seeking Norwegian funding for a package of measures aimed at reducing pressure on the village, including a park-and-ride below the hillside settlement, improved footpaths and drainage, the restoration of traditional barns and terraces, and the conversion of the former village school into a community and cultural center. The project would also create more opportunities for local residents to work as guides and custodians, he said. Is removal from the list possible? Anton Sabucha is in a minority. But even if he somehow gets his wish, having Vlkolinec struck off the World Heritage List is an almost impossible task. It looks unlikely that Vlkolinec will become the first site to be removed from the UNESCO World Heritage List at the request of its residents Image: Rob Cameron/DW UNESCO has removed sites only three times since the program was established in 1978: Germany's Dresden Elbe Valley after the construction of a four-lane bridge , Liverpool's historical waterfront following large-scale redevelopment and Oman 's Arabian Oryx Sanctuary after most of the protected reserve was stripped of its status. In each case, UNESCO acted because the sites had irreversibly lost the qualities for which they had originally been inscribed. There is no precedent for a community asking to be removed voluntarily. And there is no sign that Vlkolinec is about to become the first to succeed in its request. https://www.baltictimes.com/election_sum.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Election summer in Latvia: much uncertainty, but favorites shine 2026-07-20 Kaspars Germanis Photo: Kaspars Germanis is a researcher at the Center for Geopolitical Studies in Riga With only a few months left until the Latvian Parliament Saeima elections, along with the traditional unpredictability - how currently undecided citizens will vote - others are also coming into play. First, how will Latvia pass the Russian test in defense, and second, it is unclear how the new government, appointed in May, will work. However, some potential leaders are emerging. The new government raises the temperature With just a few months left until the Saeima elections on October 3, the atmosphere in Latvian politics is traditionally heating up. The approval of the new government on May 28 is also adding spice. Assuming the post-election government is approved in November, its lifespan could be approximately six months. However, the government was not formed until February 2019, following the 2018 elections. The new Cabinet of Ministers is headed by the previous MP Andris Kulbergs (“United List”), who had earned recognition for his actions and statements, especially regarding such very serious issues in Latvia as the future of the international railway project “Rail Baltica” . No one knows yet how Kulbergs and his four-party coalition (the “United List”, the National Alliance, the Greens and Farmers’ Union, and the “New Unity”) will work together and which of its members will be the winners and losers. Under the power of difficult decisions Although the life of the Kulbergs’ government is predictably short, it will not be able to avoid difficult decisions. Kulbergs and his ministers will have to decide what to do with the national airline “airBaltic”. Already now, there is a belief that “airBaltic” will not be able to survive if the government does not allocate additional funds from the Latvian budget. In a situation where Latvia intends to devote almost 5% of its GDP to defense, and in addition, problems in education, social welfare, and other fields have not disappeared anywhere, allocating additional millions to “airBaltic” may question the popularity of Kultberg’s government. Besides, Russia will likely continue to test Latvia’s defense capabilities, which means that there will be more drone strikes. Other hybrid warfare methods are not ruled out. If the Kulbergs’ government and the coalition parties can defend the country, then it could be a significant psychological victory. Moreover, after the scandal in the Riga City Council elections last year, when the electronic voting machine broke, there is no certainty that Russia could not use the disruption of elections by damaging electronic systems. Foggy forecasts The party popularity ratings published in May show that 27.2% citizens have not decided which party they are going to support. Moreover, 13.2% claim, at least currently, that they will not participate in the elections. This means that the fight for votes in the summer will be brutal. And yet, despite everything, the approximate outlines of the next Saeima can be predicted. One can safely predict the entry of the experienced politician Ainārs Šlesers’ party “Latvia First” into parliament, and, possibly, even victory. This party has support among both Latvian and Russian-speaking voters. On the other hand, some voters have not forgotten him as an “oligarch”, as he has been called for years. It is not excluded that “Latvia First” will suffer the fate of the once popular party “Harmony”. It also won the Saeima elections, but was so toxic to the so-called Latvian parties that it always remained in opposition. The number of mandates in the next Saeima will be won by the National Alliance, “Progressives” and “Sovereign Power”. All three have a sufficiently stable voter base. The National Alliance continues to attract nationalists, the “Progressives” – very liberal and left-wing, especially young and middle-aged voters, the “Sovereign Power” – Russian-speaking voters, and probably more of those who would like to see friendly relations between Latvia and Russia. It is expected that the Greens and Farmers’ Union, which have always had support in the countryside, will enter the next Saeima, also with a similar number of mandates. The “New Unity” will also enter the Saeima with a smaller number of mandates than it currently has. Heavily criticized, there are still enough national-conservative and pro-Western voters in Latvia. It is most likely that the “United List” will also enter the next Saeima, whose recognition will be significantly improved by working in the new coalition. However, once again, this summer in Latvian politics has been particularly hot and unpredictable for various reasons. This means that these forecasts may have to be completely changed in the second half of September. Comments Related Articles Subscribe Log In Ads Please enter your username and password. https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/08/21/esza.text: Menü Kereső Az Északi Áramlat felrobbantásáról szóló film forgatásán vették őrizetbe az észak-áramlat felrobbantásával gyanúsított ukrán férfit Külföld Ignácz Péter Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Egy, az Északi Áramlat felrobbantásáról szóló hollywoodi film pulai forgatásán dolgozott tanácsadóként az az ukrán férfit, akit a gázvezeték felrobbantásának gyanújával vettek őrizetbe Horvátországban – írta a Guardian és a horvát sajtó , a Legal Tribute Online (LTO) német igazságügyi magazinra hivatkozva. A férfi letartóztatását szerdán jelentette be a német ügyészség. Az ügyészség szerint „egy képzett búvár, aki tagja volt azon személyek csoportjának, akik robbanószereket helyeztek el az Északi Áramlat 1 és az Északi Áramlat 2 földgázvezetékein a dániai Bornholm-sziget közelében 2022 szeptemberében”. Egy horvátországi bíróság elrendelte a férfi előzetes őrizetbe helyezését, amíg az európai körözés alapján döntenek kiadatásáról Németországnak – írta az MTI. Volodimir Zsuravljov a beszámoló szerint tanácsadóként dolgozott a Jason Bourne filmeket is készítő Doug Liman rendező filmjének forgatásán , ami ukrán búvárok egy csoportjáról szól, akik szabotázsakciókat hajtanak végre. A szereplők közt van Sean Penn, valamint Adrien Brody is. Az egyelőre nem lehet tudni, hogy ki szólt a horvát hatóságoknak az ukrán férfi szerepéről a forgatáson – írta a Guardian. A férfit tavaly szeptemberben Lengyelországban már letartóztattak , de kiadatását Németországnak végül egy lengyel bíróság elutasította , arra hivatkozva, hogy a németek alig indokolták meg a kiadatást, valamint hogy az ukránok „igazságos, védekező háborút” vívnak, aminek során az ellenség infrastruktúráját támadták. Ezt Donald Tusk lengyel kormányfő is támogatta. Tavaly nyáron Olaszországban vettek őrizetbe egy ukrán férfit, akit pár hónappal később kiadtak Németországnak, ahol az ügyészek július elején vádat emeltek ellene a gázvezetékek felrobbantása miatt. A német ügyészség közölte azt is, hogy Szerhij K., aki akkor az ukrán hadsereg tisztje volt, más katonákkal együtt „ az ukrán állami hatóságok parancsára ” dolgozta ki az Északi Áramlat 1 és 2 gázvezetékek megsemmisítésére irányuló tervet. Az Északi Áramlat gázvezetéket 2022 szeptemberében robbantották fel. A Wall Street Journal két évvel később az ukrán vezetést nevezte meg az Északi Áramlat gázvezeték felrobbantásának értelmi szerzőjeként és végrehajtójaként, azután, hogy Németország körözést adott ki egy ukrán állampolgárral szemben, aki részt vehetett az akcióban. A 2022-es támadás lényegesen korlátozta az Európába irányuló orosz gázszállítást. Az akciót, ami komoly eszkalációt jelentett az orosz–ukrán háborúban, a nyugati országok és Oroszország is szabotázsként írták le.
